explanations.explanation: Foes it is, friend. David opens with, "O LORD, how my foes have increased!" (Psalm 3:1). He doesn't dress it up or pretend things are fine. He just tells the LORD how things really are, and I think that's a good way to start a prayer.
Flocks would be a lovely problem to have. But the verse never mentions sheep. David says, "O LORD, how my foes have increased!" (Psalm 3:1). More fluffy neighbors would have been a nicer headline.
A bigger field would be nice news, but that's not what David reports. He says, "how my foes have increased!" (Psalm 3:1). The count that grew was his enemies, and he tells the LORD about it plainly.

That's the line, friend. David says, "Many say of me, 'God will not deliver him.'" (Psalm 3:2). It's a heavy thing to hear about yourself. Notice that David tells it to God and doesn't keep it to himself.

explanations.answer: God has chosen a new king
explanations.explanation: The psalm says nothing about a new king. What David reports is, "Many say of me, 'God will not deliver him.'" (Psalm 3:2). That's the whole message, and it's about whether God will rescue him. A new king doesn't come up at all.

The heading names Absalom, since David fled from his son (Psalm 3:1). But the people's words aren't about whose side God is on. They say, "God will not deliver him." (Psalm 3:2). Stick with what the text says and you'll be fine.

A shield, friend. David says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me" (Psalm 3:3). Look at that word "around." I think a shield you can hold in front of you is good, but one all the way around is even better.

A lamp is handy for finding the cookie jar at midnight, but it isn't David's picture here. He says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me" (Psalm 3:3). With foes rising up, a shield is the image he reaches for.

David doesn't say the LORD is a river. He says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me" (Psalm 3:3). A river might water the garden, but a shield is what he names. It's a short verse, so it's easy to hold onto.

True. David says the LORD is "my glory, and the One who lifts my head." (Psalm 3:3). He says it right after hearing what many were saying about him. I think a lifted head is a mighty fine thing to have in a rough week.

This one is actually true. David says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head." (Psalm 3:3). So he does call the LORD the One who lifts his head. Easy to second-guess when the crowd is so loud in verse 2.
Not quite, friend. David says, "To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain." (Psalm 3:4). So the LORD answers him. Silence isn't in this verse at all.
False is right. David says, "To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain." (Psalm 3:4). He cries out, and the LORD answers. I love that David didn't mumble it.

That's the reason David gives. He says, "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me." (Psalm 3:5). Lie down, sleep, wake up, and the reason is the LORD. I'd sleep better with that reason, honestly.
The psalm never mentions guards. David gives his reason: "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me." (Psalm 3:5). The LORD is the One he names, and nobody else is on the list.

David never says they're far away. A little later he talks about "the myriads set against me on every side" (Psalm 3:6). His reason for sleeping and waking is this: "for the LORD sustains me." (Psalm 3:5).
Fear is the word. David says, "I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side." (Psalm 3:6). Myriads means a huge number, and he still says it. That's some steady courage, friend.
David never says he won't count them. He says, "I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side." (Psalm 3:6). Counting that many would take forever anyway, and the verse is about fear.

David doesn't say anything about fighting here. He says, "I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side." (Psalm 3:6). The word is fear, and the next verse is a prayer: "Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!" (Psalm 3:7).
Save him, friend. David prays, "Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!" (Psalm 3:7). It's short and it's direct. I like a prayer that gets right to it.
David doesn't ask to be hidden. His words are, "Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!" (Psalm 3:7). He asks to be saved. Hiding isn't in the request.
Forgiveness isn't what he asks for in this verse. He says, "Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!" (Psalm 3:7). So his request here is to be saved.
True, and it's right there in the text. David prays, "Strike all my enemies on the jaw" (Psalm 3:7). It's blunt, and he says it to the LORD. I think that's honest praying, with nothing held back.

This one is true, friend. David prays, "Strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked." (Psalm 3:7). The jaw is in the verse. It's a plain-spoken prayer, and he brings it straight to the LORD.
The LORD, friend. David says, "Salvation belongs to the LORD" (Psalm 3:8). After all that talk of enemies, he ends on who saves. It's a great last line.
David is a king, but that's not who he names. He says, "Salvation belongs to the LORD" (Psalm 3:8). He closes by pointing past himself, which I think is a humble way to end.
Priests don't appear in this psalm. David says, "Salvation belongs to the LORD" (Psalm 3:8). He gives it to the LORD alone, and then he prays for God's people.

Not quite, friend. David ends with, "Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people." (Psalm 3:8). He prays for God's people, and that's more than just himself. Notice how far his prayer reaches.

False is right. David closes with, "Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people." (Psalm 3:8). He asks for blessing on God's people, not just on himself. A prayer that began with his foes ends with the whole people of God.
